Fan jackets become main product at Sham Shui Po Apliu Street hardware stores, cheapest priced at $298, most expensive nearly $1,000

At 2:44pm in Sham Shui Po, with temperatures reaching 35.5 degrees, at Apliu Street lined with hardware stores, reporters observed on-site that many shops were hanging various "fan jackets", ranging from long-sleeve to short-sleeve, fluorescent workwear styles or jacket styles, with brands from the mainland, Canada, and Japan. Among the more than ten shops the reporter passed, some only priced the jackets, ranging from tens to over a hundred dollars, while others labeled full-set prices ranging from $298 to $980.

Air-conditioning unit installed on the back

The reporter inquired as a customer and found that the "fan jacket" consists of three parts: fan, battery, and jacket. Apart from different jacket styles, batteries are categorized by adapter capacity and voltage levels (12, 24, 30V), as well as the number of fans equipped. One shop's fan jacket was priced at $498, and the staff also introduced to the reporter a "air-conditioning jacket" model, saying it has a small air-conditioning unit installed on the back, with the full set totaling $698.

"We go back to the construction site now, and they (workers) will put them all on." Mr Wong, who is in the renovation trade, was at a stall in Apliu Street today choosing a "fan jacket". He said he noticed Japan launching the product first two or three years ago, "at that time we had to find ways to get Japanese purchasing agents...including the original battery it cost almost $1,800."

Mr Wong said, taking himself as an example, at some construction sites windows cannot be opened, with only hard-to-move pedestal fans for circulation, easily reaching over 30 degrees. Added to that, workers may not pay attention to the "Work Heat Stress at Work Warning" rest periods, so they tend to help themselves. "People say, 'You still buy it even though it's so expensive?' At that time there was Taobao, but the fans only had 5V back then...you just feel that thing is necessary." He said he is aware of the Labour Department's "Heat Protection Products Subsidy Scheme", but the application process is complicated and requires waiting for approval, so it's better to simply buy fan jackets for employees.

Stall specializing in fan jackets sells nearly 100 sets daily

August 9 saw the hottest day on record, but Mr Chung, owner of a stall specializing in "fan jackets", said sales began to increase from early March this year; recently nearly 100 sets of "fan jackets" are sold daily. Currently Mr Chung's customers are mainly construction site workers, and recently food delivery workers have also been patronizing. "Many times it's a last-minute thing...many customers come to buy when they're almost getting heatstroke or feeling dizzy."

He said cleaners only account for a small portion of customers, mainly private property cleaners, which he believes is related to outsourced cleaners needing to wear standard uniforms. He said, taking a "fan jacket" equipped with a 30,000 mAh battery as an example, it can run for 8 hours at medium fan speed. Many workers directly purchase the most expensive model because it has "more fan positions" and can cool down more effectively.

Park snack kiosk owner records 39 degrees before turning on stove, closes shop to visit Sham Shui Po to buy "fan jacket"

Besides workers, Ms Cheung, a park snack kiosk tenant, was also making a purchase outside Mr Chung's stall.

"I went back to my shop this morning and it was 39 degrees, I hadn't even turned on the stove, I couldn't take it so I had to come buy one to try." Ms Cheung said working at the snack kiosk with no air-conditioning, she used an infrared thermometer to measure the outside wall at 37 degrees, and inside the 150-square-foot snack kiosk, the ceiling reached a maximum of 41 degrees.

She said with a smile that she only learned from the radio that the Work Heat Stress at Work Warning was in effect, but for her the warning is "useless", "because we are tenants, whether you cook or not we have to open the shop, if we don't open we still have to pay rent." Coming to Sham Shui Po to look for treasures, she also learned about it through word of mouth from construction site workers, "You can't save this kind of money, whatever it takes you have to think of a way."

The Hong Kong Observatory issued the Very Hot Weather Warning from 6:45am on August 5 until now, and recorded a record-breaking 36.9 degrees on August 9. The Labour Department has issued the Yellow Work Heat Stress at Work Warning seven times from August 4 to now. Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying and the public questioned the effectiveness of the mechanism. Labour Department Commissioner Hui Chak-sum responded for the first time today on a radio programme, saying that the mechanism did not escalate to a higher level as expected, "We also have many question marks."
